Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
Muhammad Danish Waseem * 1 Ahmed Ali-Eldin Hassan * 1

Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions. However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot real-time requirements for its next action. To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis on what are the real bottlenecks for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimization would generalize beyond the reported results. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another. From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets. The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required saving and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are multimodal models that enable robots to translate visual observations and natural-language instructions into executable actions, such as moving an arm or opening a gripper. They typically build on pretrained vision-language models that are trained on robot demonstrations, connecting visual and semantic knowledge with the physical skills needed to perform tasks Zitkovich and others (2023) .
VLAs aim to support general-purpose robots that can follow diverse instructions and generalize to unfamiliar objects and environments Kim et al. (2024) ; Intelligence et al. (2025) .

Internally, VLAs typically run a VLM with millions or billions of parameters to generate the robot’s control steps. This limits the reaction time of a robot by the inference latency of the VLA. At each policy inference step, a typical VLA receives a natural-language instruction, represented as text, and image observations from one or more cameras. In a common architecture, a vision encoder converts camera images into visual embeddings, which are projected into the language model’s embedding space and processed jointly with the instruction tokens by a transformer backbone. The resulting representations condition the prediction of a robot action or a short sequence of actions with the action generations performed using an action-head.

VLAs need to be real-time, providing a robot with a sufficient number of actions such that the robot does not stall. Robots typically operate with strictly bounded latencies to maintain a continuous, closed-loop feedback cycle. In addition, if a VLA is too slow, it acts on stale visual data, i.e., by the time the model computes and outputs a command, the physical world has already changed leading to dropped objects, collisions, or unstable movement. This is challenging, especially when the VLA is running on the limited on-robot hardware. One approach to reduce the computational time of VLAs is to use optimization methods such as, token pruning, quantization, compilation, or CUDA graphs. However, our study of 25 published paper (Appendix E ) reveals that most of these approaches do not consider the intricacies of the different VLA architectures and the hardware they run on.

VLAs today vary in architecture, backbone size, visual token count and action path. These choices decide which stage dominates latency and therefore which optimization can help. The backbone size sets how many weight bytes every pass must read, so a large model could spend most of its time reading the model weights, whereas a smaller model could spend its time in the denoising loop of action head. In addition, previous work on VLA optimizations does not consider the inherent bottlenecks of the underlying hardware platform projecting generality of the results while only evaluating the work on a limited set of hardware. For example, many previous works evaluate the optimizations on GPUs such as NVIDIA RTX 4090s, a GPU that has a heavy weight and high power draw—it is neither designed for running on a robot platform nor is available on most clouds, hence, not supporting a cloud-robotic deployment.

In this work, we provide a comprehensive study of VLA optimization performance. We start by analyzing seven families of inference optimization methods, namely; CUDA graphs, compilation, fused attention, batching, reducing the denoising steps, token pruning and quantization. We evaluate these optimizations on seven VLAs, namely; OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, LLaVA-VLA, CogACT, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , GR00T, and SmolVLA, with four kinds of action head (token decoding, parallel decoding, diffusion, flow matching). These combinations are then tested on four different GPU families; a datacenter grade H100, a cloud A10G, a consumer RTX 4090, and an embedded Jetson Thor.
Our evaluations focus on the latency gains of these optimizations, showing that the optimization results are non-uniform. Gains differ between GPUs in magnitude, in sign and in rank.

For example, compiling GR00T with CUDA graphs makes it faster on the H100 and slower on the Thor, and storing CogACT’s weights in 8 bits makes it faster on the A10G and slower on the H100. In addition, we find that the choice of baseline to compare an optimization method to can be misleading, e.g., FastV Chen et al. (2024) and several other token pruning methods (Appendix E ) select the visual tokens to prune by their attention weights, so it is typically evaluated and compared to running with unfused attention. However, VLAs in production are often deployed with fused attention kernels such as FlashAttention-2 Dao (2024) , which never write attention weights to memory. Measured against unfused attention, FastV at 50 50 % pruning saves 21.4 21.4 % of OpenVLA-OFT’s inference time on an H100. Measured against FlashAttention-2, the same run saves 6.9 6.9 %, because the selector reads attention weights and forces the slower kernel (Table 5 ).

Our analysis also shows that each stage of inference is limited by either the GPU compute power, its memory bandwidth, or the CPU that launches the GPU kernels. This means that the same stage can be subject to a different bottleneck on different GPUs. Therefore, a proposed optimization method’s benefit may not extend beyond the platform it is tested on.

In addition, optimization methods can be combined, or stacked. Hence, running multiple optimizations in sequence means that later VLA optimizations act on the inference stages that are left by previous optimizations. Hence, the total gains from a later method depends on the methods applied before it. Based on the above observations, we formalize VLA-Triage , a systematic approach for evaluating the expected gains of multiple VLA optimization methods on a given hardware. To summarize, our paper has three connected contributions:

Characterisation : paired measurements of inference-stage costs and optimization benefits across seven VLAs and four GPU-host platforms, including cases where a method helps on one platform and hurts on another.
Interactions : We show how graphs, compilation and pruning change the gains for later applied methods, and how reusing standalone gains can change latency-budget decisions.
Guidelines : A measurement-based workflow for choosing an execution mode, checking feasibility under stated assumptions, and validating method combinations to be used in deployment.

VLA inference has three main stages. First, a vision encoder converts images into visual tokens. After that, the language backbone processes these tokens together with the task instructions; this stage is called prefill. Finally, an action-generation stage produces the robot’s commands. A chunk is a sequence of actions produced by one inference, so the robot can execute several control steps before requesting another prediction. One of the main differences between VLA models is in how they generate actions. This can be categorized in three main model categories:

Autoregressive decoding models , e.g., OpenVLA Kim et al. (2024) and LLaVA-VLA Song et al. (2026) : Represent actions as a sequence of tokens, generated one per forward pass. Repeated passes read the language-model weights, making memory transfers, CPU kernel launches, and kernel performance important.

Prefill-heavy models , e.g., OpenVLA-OFT Kim et al. (2025) and CogACT Li et al. (2024) : Run the language backbone once during prefill. OpenVLA-OFT predicts a chunk using action placeholder tokens processed in parallel. CogACT feeds prefill embeddings into a small diffusion transformer sampled with DDIM, a diffusion sampling method Song et al. (2020) .

Iterative flow models , e.g., π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} Intelligence et al. (2025) , GR00T Bjorck et al. (2025) , SmolVLA Shukor et al. (2025) : Refine an action chunk through multiple flow-matching steps Lipman et al. (2022) , using a small action network. We measured with four steps for GR00T and ten for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and SmolVLA.

The inference deadline depends on how the robot consumes its actions. A single-action policy must finish inference within one control period Δ \Delta , which is set by the robot motor frequencies. With asynchronous execution, a chunked policy computes the next chunk while the robot executes actions already in an action queue Black et al. (2026) . This can lead to the VLA acting on stale video data. Hence the number of actions should not be too large such that the robot will fail due to working on stale video data, or too few such that the robot movements are sluggish due to the VLA inference time.

We model the chunking policy through the asynchronous scheduler of LeRobot Cadene et al. (2026) , which initiates inference when A r A_{r} actions remain in the robot’s execution queue. Figure 2 maps the methods to the work they change. For interpreting performance, we distinguish methods that remove repeated work from those that change the GPU kernels used. Work-removing methods eliminate repeated operations. CUDA graphs NVIDIA (2026a) reduce repeated CPU launches by replaying recorded kernel sequences. Visual token pruning Chen et al. (2024) removes image tokens after early layers. Step reduction Tang et al. (2026) ; Luan et al. (2026) removes denoising passes in the action head. Kernel-replacing methods change how the GPU executes the computation. torch.compile Ansel et al. () fuses operations and generates kernels. Fused attention avoids writing large attention matrices to memory. Quantization Park et al. (2024) compresses weights (int8, int4) or uses lower-precision arithmetic (FP8, int8). A quantization scheme specifies weight and activation precision, together with a scaling rule. Weight-only quantization retains bf16 (16-bit floating-point) activations; int8 compute uses int8 weights and activations for matrix multiplication. FP8 and NVFP4 use 8-bit and 4-bit floating-point values, respectively. Different quantization schemes can use different kernel libraries. Batching processes requests together, sharing weight reads to improve throughput.

We call graphs, compilation and fused attention accuracy-neutral because they preserve the intended computation up to numerical rounding. We call pruning, step reduction, and quantization accuracy-risking , as they change the computation and require task-specific accuracy evaluation.

We evaluate the inference optimization methods shown in Figure 2 , with seven VLA models listed in Table 1 . Table 7 in Appendix lists the four GPU-host systems we tested with, along with their software versions, measured throughput, bandwidth and CPU launch costs.
We measure the time starting after CPU image preprocessing and ending when the model returns its actions.
We validate that the model’s input and output remain valid during measurements (details in Appendix A).

We compare three execution modes. 1) In eager execution, PyTorch launches operations as they run. 2) CUDA graphs replay recorded GPU work with a single CPU launch. 3) torch.compile is used with its reduce-overhead option, which also uses CUDA graphs where supported, and its max-autotune option, which also benchmarks alternative matrix-multiplication kernels. The Llama-family VLA stages are compiled separately so that CUDA events can still time them, with decode served by one graph over a fixed-size masked cache. OpenPi ships π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} with the whole call compiled, and we keep that scope. For GR00T we compile the DiT action loop, which takes most of the inference time, and leave the Qwen3-VL backbone eager. For SmolVLA, compiling the whole call has no effect. Its vision embedding selects tokens with a mask computed from the image, so the resulting shape is only known at runtime. The compiler cannot trace such an operation, and torch.compile would then run the entire function eagerly. We therefore compile only the denoising step, which runs ten times per inference.

We keep each VLA’s attention backend as released. The Llama models use FlashAttention-2 Dao (2024) , GR00T and SmolVLA use scaled dot-product attention (SDPA), and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} uses unfused attention with OpenPi’s explicit prefix-LM mask, which the fused kernels do not accept. Accuracy-neutral modes are compared against eager execution. Token pruning and step reduction are evaluated against the unpruned and full-step baseline, respectively, in the same execution mode.

Quantization is compared in two execution modes. The main comparison (Table 8 ) uses reduce-overhead compilation, with the bf16 baseline measured in the same mode as the quantised runs. A separate comparison measures the same schemes under CUDA graphs without compilation, to separate the gain of the quantised kernels from the gain the compiler adds by fusing their scaling and casting. Only language-backbone linear layers are quantised. For each quantization scheme and platform, we time the available library implementations and use the fastest one whose output error stays within 1.25 times the smallest error among them (Table 9 ).

Short GPU kernels make latency sensitive to CPU launch delays. We pin the issuing process to an idle CPU core near the GPU and warm up before timing. Each measurement round repeats the job’s selected configurations. We report medians of at least 200 inferences per configuration, or 100 batches for batching. Across repeated jobs, the median latency difference is 0.2% under CUDA graphs and 1.4% in eager execution (Appendix B ). The largest eager baseline change we observed, when remeasuring the RTX 4090 baselines, is 5.3% (Appendix B ).

We test whether a saving measured before an optimization remains applicable after it. We call this measurement reuse. We ask whether the earlier optimization changes the GPU work. We call a change execution-preserving if it mainly removes CPU launches while retaining GPU kernels and their input dimensions, otherwise it is execution-altering . Compilation, pruning and quantization fall in the latter group. The distinctions serve different purposes. Accuracy-neutral or risking indicates whether task validation is needed. Work-removing or kernel-replacing describes what the method changes. Execution-preserving or altering indicates whether eager measurements may remain informative.

If an optimization changes only the stage it targets, accelerating a fraction σ \sigma of baseline latency by a factor s s saves an overall fraction g = σ ⁡ ( 1 − 1 / s ) g=\sigma(1-1/s) of baseline time. Here the stage share σ \sigma is the fraction of inference time spent in the affected stage, and s s is its speed-up. We use the identity to explain measured changes. An earlier optimization can change the stage share σ \sigma , the speed-up s s , or both. For instance, once compilation shortens the action loop, it lowers action head share σ \sigma , leaving fewer denoising steps less time to save. Similarly, pruning lowers the share of prefill layers and also changes their matrix sizes, and with them the speed-up s s of the quantised kernels applied to them. Section 5 examines these effects.

(2009) (Figure 3 ) compares arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) with the ridge point C / B ​ W C/BW , where the idealised memory and compute references cross. For a bf16 linear layer with n n parameters and M M tokens, 2 ​ M ​ n 2Mn operations and 2 ​ n 2n weight bytes give an intensity near M M when weight reads dominate; long prefills can approach the compute limit, while single-token decoding ( M = 1 M=1 ) lies on the memory side .

Figure 3: Stage throughput against each platform’s roofline reference, unpruned bf16 at batch one. Colour denotes the model and shape denotes the stage. Arithmetic intensity uses the operator traffic of Equation ( 2 ).

Figure 3 shows the roofline model for the different stages of the seven VLAs on the four GPUs. Autoregressive decoding approaches the memory reference on A10G and Thor. H100 leaves more headroom. On the H100, a decoded Llama-2-7B token takes 9.6 ms under graphs (Table 4 ) against a 3.7 ms weight-read reference at the measured bandwidth. Each pass issues well over a thousand kernels. Compilation with max-autotune reduces kernel counts and brings the time per decoded token to 5.7 ms. Many of these kernels are short elementwise and normalisation operations that move little data and leave DRAM bandwidth underused, so fusing them closes part of the gap. The measurements do not isolate how much of the remaining gap each kernel accounts for. All Thor stages lie left of the ridge point under this traffic estimate, where memory cost exceeds compute cost in the reference.

The gap to measured performance can include kernel inefficiency, CPU launches and differences in actual traffic, so position in Figure 3 alone does not establish the bottleneck. Appendix Figure 8 helps interpret stage costs using measured graph savings, estimated overhead for flow models, compute and memory reference costs, and the unexplained remainder. The flow-model estimates do not isolate CPU waiting. Graphs can reduce launch delays, pruning can reduce token-dependent work, and quantization can reduce weight traffic or change arithmetic costs. Their opportunities therefore depend on which costs remain.

For the Llama-based models, CUDA graphs save more where the estimated idle share I / T I/T is larger (Appendix Figure 9 ). The idle share is the fraction of eager inference time in which no GPU kernel is running. On the A10G and Thor, decode loops spend more time reading weights and gain little from graphs. The saving depends on whether the CPU can launch the next kernel before the GPU finishes its current work.

Figure 4: Latency benefits and memory costs of accuracy-neutral methods. (a) Speed-up of reduce-overhead compilation over CUDA graphs alone for the four Llama-based models. The RTX 4090 shows compilation without graphs. Bar labels give the eager kernel count divided by the compiled count. (b) GPU memory beyond the model weights at batch sizes one and eight, medians over the GPUs where the configuration fits. The CUDA-graphs bars hold one graph. The four-level bars hold one graph per pruning level, each with its own memory pool, and at batch eight OpenVLA-OFT and LLaVA-VLA then exceed the 24GB of an RTX 4090 or A10G.

Compilation fuses elementwise and normalisation operations, reducing kernel counts by 1.9 × 1.9\times to 2.8 × 2.8\times in our experiments, and providing additional speed-ups after CUDA graphs reduce time outside kernels. Figure 4 a shows both effects. Its bar heights give the speed-up over graphs alone, and its bar labels the ratio of eager to compiled kernel counts. Fewer kernels also means fewer launches, so the speed-up may come from launch and scheduling savings as much as from reduced DRAM traffic. Compilation also changes the preferred quantization scheme. For OpenVLA-OFT on H100, static FP8 is fastest under compilation, speeding up whole inference by 1.43 × 1.43\times over compiled bf16 and prefill alone by 1.68 × 1.68\times (Table 8 ). Under graphs without compilation it is instead the slowest of the three, at 33.5 ms against 31.5 ms for dynamic FP8 and 31.0 ms for int8 compute. Compilation changes two things at once. It fuses the scaling and casting of activations into neighbouring kernels, and it can select different matrix-multiplication kernels.

Compilation can also slow inference. For GR00T on Thor, compiler-generated copy and conversion kernels increase GPU kernel duration despite shorter gaps between kernels (“GR00T compiled on the Thor” in Appendix D ). Execution modes also require memory and setup time. Each captured graph uses fixed tensor dimensions and reserved GPU memory pools, while compilation can take minutes (Appendix Table 6 ). Figure 4 b shows the memory each execution mode needs beyond the model weights. A CUDA graph is captured for fixed tensor shapes, so a deployment that varies its batch size or pruning level at run time must keep one graph per shape resident. Each graph reserves a memory pool roughly as large as the activation memory of eager inference at that batch size. At batch eight, four pruning-level graphs held at once reserve 11 to 13 GB of pools on top of 13 to 14 GB of weights for OpenVLA-OFT or LLaVA-VLA, which exceeds the 24 GB of an RTX 4090 or A10G.
Pruning reduces token-dependent work in the language-model layers. We use random token selection to measure the latency effect of token count.

These timings measure performance at each token count. They do not determine which token-selection method preserves task accuracy. Under CUDA graphs, prefill latency generally shortens with token count (Appendix Figure 10 ). Pruning reduces token-dependent computation but does not eliminate the weight reads of layers that still run.

Fewer tokens do not always reduce latency. Matrix-multiplication (GEMM) kernels process tokens in fixed-size blocks called tiles, so removing tokens that do not empty a whole tile saves little. Some measured points even become slower as the token count falls (Appendix Figure 10 ), likely because the library selects a different kernel at the new shape. In eager execution, pruning can also stop helping once CPU launches, rather than GPU work, set the latency.
Token selection adds its own cost. FastV Chen et al. (2024) ranks visual tokens by attention weights. Obtaining those weights requires a slower, unfused attention implementation.
Table 5 compares these variants with random selection, showing that selection overhead and the attention backend directly affect the realised latency saving.

In flow and diffusion heads, each denoising step repeats a forward pass over identical action-head weights. Fewer steps shorten this loop while leaving vision and prefill unchanged. Appendix Table 4 separates the cost of one denoising step from the time outside the denoising loop. In eager execution, small action heads issue many short kernels, leaving the GPU waiting for CPU launches. Compilation accelerates individual steps in π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and SmolVLA by over 2 × 2\times , whereas GR00T’s generated kernels on Thor lengthen step time.

Quantization stores weights at lower precision. Quantization schemes that also quantize activations use lower-precision inputs for matrix multiplication. As shown in Table 8 , weight-only quantization schemes (int8, int4) accelerate memory-bandwidth-bound stages, cutting decode loop latency on the A10G and Thor. During prefill, dequantization and kernel overhead can outweigh the time saved by reading fewer weight bytes. Activation quantization schemes (FP8, int8 compute) use lower-precision tensor cores to accelerate dense prefill GEMMs. They need enough tokens for this saving to outweigh quantization and scaling overhead. A weight-only quantization scheme can therefore shorten decode while lengthening prefill in the same inference.

passages.location: 5 How One optimization Changes the Next
passages.text: A deployment may combine methods whose benefits were measured separately. We ask whether a method’s saving still holds once another optimization has been applied. We use the distinction between execution-preserving and execution-altering from Section 3.2 to interpret the results.

On a fixed model, platform and software version, we measure the baseline T 0 T_{0} , the earlier optimization alone T 1 T_{1} , the later method alone T 2 T_{2} , and both together T 12 T_{12} . The later method saves T 0 − T 2 T_{0}-T_{2} without the earlier optimization and T 1 − T 12 T_{1}-T_{12} with it. We test two assumptions about whether that saving remains unchanged. Percentage reuse assumes the later method saves the same percentage of time, giving T reuse = T 1 ​ ( T 2 / T 0 ) T_{\rm reuse}=T_{1}(T_{2}/T_{0}) . Millisecond reuse assumes it saves the same number of milliseconds, giving T reuse = T 1 − ( T 0 − T 2 ) T_{\rm reuse}=T_{1}-(T_{0}-T_{2}) . We compare the latency implied by each assumption with the measured T 12 T_{12} . An assumption is optimistic when the implied latency is lower than measured, and pessimistic when it is higher. We report cases where measured latency exceeds the implied value by more than 5.3%, the largest eager baseline change observed during remeasurement (Section 3 ).
We perfrom a case-study on three example and likely optimization sequences (summarized in Figure 5 ). These cases examine the selected sequences, not all possible optimization combinations.

CUDA graphs leave the GPU kernels unchanged. Pruning therefore removes the same token-dependent work as in eager execution. Graphs also remove launch overhead, so total inference is shorter. The kernel time that pruning removes is then a larger share of that shorter total. In eager execution part of that kernel time was hidden behind CPU launches, so the milliseconds saved change as well. The eager percentage therefore does not carry over exactly. In the recorded comparisons, measured latency under CUDA graphs ranges from 23 23 % below to less than 1 1 % above the value implied by applying pruning’s eager percentage saving unchanged. Profiles show that the small excesses involve changes in both kernel time and time outside kernels. Appendix F splits each excess into a kernel-time term and a time-outside-kernels term from the traces, and shows that both stay within about 1 ms on the H100 and A10G and largely cancel on the Thor.

LLaVA-VLA needs separate treatment because CUDA graphs change its decoding cache. Its decoding attends over a fixed-size masked cache, changing kernel timing (Section 3.2 ). LLaVA-VLA’s pruning savings must therefore be measured under CUDA graphs rather than carried over from eager execution. Figure 5 plots LLaVA-VLA in the “Graphs with cache change” row. OpenVLA uses the same cache layout, but its recorded timing changes are small, so we treat it as approximately execution-preserving.

passages.section: Case 2: Compilation, then pruning or fewer denoising steps.
passages.location: Case 2: Compilation, then pruning or fewer denoising steps.
passages.text: Compilation changes kernel execution times. This changes how much time pruning or fewer steps can save. For CogACT, 75% pruning saves 3.9 ms on H100 in eager execution and 4.1 ms after max-autotune compilation. Prefill is a small share of CogACT’s time on H100 in both modes, so pruning has little to remove either way. However, on A10G, CogACT’s saving falls from 74.2 to 33.5 ms as compilation already shortens prefill (Appendix Table 13 ). Compiler mode also matters: switching unpruned CogACT from reduce-overhead to max-autotune on A10G saves 42.7 ms, more than the subsequent pruning saves.

passages.text: In 29 of 32 flow-model comparisons, latency is more than 5.3% higher than the percentage reuse implies, reaching up to 227% higher. For SmolVLA on RTX 4090, the assumption gives 17.4 ms versus 56.9 ms measured. Carrying over the eager millisecond saving gives zero or negative latency in 21 comparisons. Pruning and step-reduction savings therefore need measurement in the chosen compiler mode.

passages.section: Case 3: Pruning, then quantization, with execution mode fixed.
passages.location: Case 3: Pruning, then quantization, with execution mode fixed.
passages.text: Pruning is work-removing because it reduces token-dependent computation. The smaller matrices can nevertheless change kernel selection and efficiency. Quantization’s benefit can change in two ways. Pruning can reduce the share of inference spent in the layers quantization accelerates, while the changed matrix sizes can raise or lower the speed-up of quantised kernels. For example, on A10G with reduce-overhead compilation, 75% pruning reduces the prefill speed-up from int8 compute for CogACT but increases it for OpenVLA-OFT (Appendix Figure 11 , Table 2 ).

passages.section: Case 3: Pruning, then quantization, with execution mode fixed.
passages.location: Case 3: Pruning, then quantization, with execution mode fixed.
passages.text: In the 194 compiled pruning–quantization configurations, measured latency exceeds the value implied by unchanged quantization percentage savings by more than 5.3% in 52, including 24 for OpenVLA-OFT on Thor. The largest discrepancy is 49%. Other configurations have lower measured latency than the assumption implies. In comparisons retaining individual token selectors, updating the affected-stage share while assuming the unpruned quantization speed-up still leaves measured latency up to about 39% above the implied value. Both the affected-stage share and quantization speed-up therefore matter (Appendix G ). quantization should be evaluated at the retained token count and in the deployed execution mode.

A change in saving can determine whether a combination meets its inference-time budget. For CogACT with 75% pruning after max-autotune compilation on A10G, assuming unchanged eager millisecond savings gives 23.3 ms, below the 50 ms budget. The measured combination takes 64.1 ms and misses it. Assuming unchanged percentage savings gives 61.4 ms, also above the budget. On H100, compilation alone takes 21.5 ms and meets the budget without pruning.

Pruning and quantization can change budget decisions too. For CogACT on A10G with int4 weights and 75% pruning in reduce-overhead mode, assuming unchanged quantization percentage savings gives 48.5 ms, within the 50 ms budget. The combination measures 59.3 ms and misses it. With 87.5% pruning in max-autotune mode, the same assumption gives 59.2 ms, above the budget, while the combination meets it at 49.2 ms. Using the same assumption would therefore lead to the wrong budget decision in both examples. Appendix Table 3 gives further examples from earlier measurements, and Appendix Table 15 gives the full budget comparison. These checks concern inference time. Section 6 adds reserves for preprocessing, communication, and scheduling.

We also examine whether a method’s measured speed-up persists across platforms. Among the selected model–method settings, none of the 14 work-removing comparisons changes from a speed-up to a slowdown across platforms, while 6 of the 21 kernel-replacing comparisons do. With matching PyTorch versions on H100 and A10G, the counts are 0 of 14 work-removing comparisons and 3 of 13 kernel-replacing comparisons. Host CPUs and other software components still differ, so these comparisons do not isolate GPU architecture. At 25% pruning, compiled π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} becomes faster on the other tested platforms but slower on Thor. The Thor slowdown appears in two separate measurement jobs.
These cases show that a later method’s benefit depends on how much of inference it can shorten and how efficiently the remaining work executes.

VLA-Triage is a set of guidelines based on the findings of Sections 4 and 5 that can be used by practitioners for deploying (or evaluating) their VLA optimizations.
1. Set the budget. For deployment, reserve time for preprocessing, communication and scheduling delays within B B :
B model = B − t preproc − t comm − t margin . B_{\rm model}=B-t_{\rm preproc}-t_{\rm comm}-t_{\rm margin}. (3)

Here B model B_{\rm model} is the time left for model execution, and t margin t_{\rm margin} reserves time for scheduling delays and latency variation. The examples below set t comm = 0 t_{\rm comm}=0 and t margin = 0.05 ​ B t_{\rm margin}=0.05B . Tables that compare measured inference T T with B B rather than B model B_{\rm model} exclude these reserves.

2. Choose execution mode. Benchmark the supported execution modes (eager, CUDA graphs, and compilation) and attention backends on the physical target. The attention backend belongs here because it is accuracy-neutral. In the recorded comparisons the best fused backend was never slower than unfused attention on any platform, whether the gain was marginal or substantial, and it lowers attention-heavy prefill, so step 2 selects a fused backend together with the execution mode. Select the fastest mode that satisfies platform memory and setup constraints (Section 4.1 ). Use its total latency T T and stage timings for the checks in step 3, because eager stage shares need not remain valid after compilation. If the selected mode alone meets B model B_{\rm model} , skip steps 3 and 4 and go to step 5.
3. Screen unviable candidates.

Weight-read screen. If reading mandatory weights alone takes longer than B model B_{\rm model} , no faster kernel can make the candidate meet the budget under the same memory traffic. Let W p 4 W_{p}^{4} be the bytes of the vision-language-model weights read in forward pass p p , counted at four bits, the lowest weight precision among the evaluated quantization schemes. This gives quantization an optimistic reference, since higher-precision weights require at least as many bytes. These weights must be streamed from DRAM on every pass. Dividing their volume by datasheet memory bandwidth B ​ W data BW_{\rm data} gives a lower bound on latency:
L w = ∑ p W p 4 B ​ W data . L_{\rm w}=\frac{\sum_{p}W_{p}^{4}}{BW_{\rm data}}. (4)

If L w > B model L_{\rm w}>B_{\rm model} , no pruning or quantization setting can meet the budget, since all of them still read these weights. Only candidates that remove reads, by caching weights or dropping layers or passes, remain, and they need their own bound.

Affected-stage screen. Each method can only shorten the stages it acts on. Pruning acts on prefill. Quantization acts on the vision-language-model layers. Step reduction acts on the action loop of the flow models. Let L m L_{m} be the latency of method m m at its strongest setting. For pruning this is inference with all visual tokens removed, which still runs the vision encoder, the text tokens and decoding. For step reduction it is inference with one denoising step, which still runs vision and prefill. No milder setting is faster, so L m L_{m} is a lower bound for method m m alone. If L m > B model L_{m}>B_{\rm model} , skip m m as a standalone candidate. A pair of methods acts on more stages than either method alone, so this screen does not exclude pairs.
4. Test supported combinations.

A pruning level is the percentage of visual tokens removed. Mild levels are tested first because they risk less accuracy. If the mode selected in step 2 is CUDA graphs, which largely preserve GPU work, eager pruning timings estimate which levels can meet the budget, through the percentage-saving assumption of Case 1 in Section 5.1 . Select initial levels whose implied latency, T 1 ​ T 2 / T 0 T_{1}T_{2}/T_{0} , is at most ( 1 + δ ) ​ B model (1+\delta)B_{\rm model} . In the recorded comparisons this estimate was usually above the measured latency under CUDA graphs, so a level whose estimate slightly exceeds the budget may still meet it. The allowance δ \delta keeps such levels in the initial set. We use δ = 5.3 % \delta=5.3\% , the largest eager baseline change observed during remeasurement (Section 3 ), and Appendix H tests other values.

If the selected mode is compilation, eager timings cannot be used to skip evaluations, because Case 2 shows that their savings need not carry over. Measure pruning and step-reduction settings in the compiled mode, from the smallest change upwards.

Quantization schemes are chosen based on hardware support and task accuracy requirements. Measure them in the deployed mode at the retained token count, because pruning can increase or decrease their benefit (Case 3). If neither pruning nor quantization meets the budget alone, test pairs.

5. Validate task performance. For each candidate meeting the latency budget, check success on the chosen benchmark and control stability in deployment. If either fails, return to step 4 to test further candidates, including further levels or pairs.

Meeting the budget with headroom. For OpenVLA-OFT on the Thor, the budget is 150 ms. Reserving recorded serial preprocessing (7.1 ms) and 5% of B B leaves 135.4 ms for model execution. Step 2 selects compilation, with a model latency of 152.6 ms (Figure 6 ). Removing 50% of visual tokens drops model time to 97.6 ms. Pruning alone therefore meets the latency budget, so the next step is task validation rather than adding quantization.

A combination that fails once reserves are included. For CogACT on A10G, the 50 ms budget leaves only 40.5 ms for inference after 7.0 ms of serial preprocessing and a 5% reserve. Max-autotune takes 97.5 ms. Prefill accounts for 72.3% of that time, enough that the affected-stage screen does not rule out pruning alone. Removing 75% of visual tokens takes 64.1 ms, and int8 compute alone takes 67.0 ms. Together they take 49.6 ms. Although the pair meets the inference-only 50 ms comparison, it exceeds the time available in deployment. The fastest recorded setting, 87.5% pruning with int8 compute, still takes 46.4 ms. None of the recorded settings meets this deployment budget, so using one would require a longer control period. Appendix Table 17 reports the other cases with and without reserves.
Spare latency can support batching or a higher control rate, subject to renewed latency and control checks (Appendix Table 10 ).

Latency predictors and tensor compilers already account for operator fusion and shape-dependent kernel selection Zhang et al. (2021) ; Wang et al. (2020) ; Chen et al. (2018) ; Zheng et al. (2020) , so a saving measured in one execution mode is known not to transfer to another. VLA acceleration papers usually do not report the mode. We audit 25 VLA acceleration papers (Appendix E ). Only one states the execution mode of both baseline and the method. None of the token-pruning, reuse, merging, or sparsification entries do, and only one of them identifies its attention backend. Readers therefore cannot check whether a reported saving applies to their execution mode.

VLA-Perf Jiang et al. (2026b) models architectural and deployment choices with an analytical roofline to estimate ideal compute and memory bounds. The XPU study Zhou et al. (2026) benchmarks VLAs across GPUs, an Intel XPU and Ascend NPUs, measuring compilation and a few method pairs, without testing methods against latency budgets. Jung et al. (2026) characterise stage balance on an RTX 4090 and two Jetson SoCs and compare per-stage compilation with eager execution, but compilation is the only model-level optimization they measure.

Our paired measurements track how a method’s benefit varies across models and GPU-host systems, and how an earlier optimization changes a later method’s saving. We examine graphs before pruning, compilation before pruning or step reduction, and pruning before quantization, then test how the differences affect latency-budget decisions.

A VLA optimization’s benefit depends on the model, GPU-host platform and methods already applied. Across seven VLAs and four platforms, our measurements show how CPU launch costs, memory costs and kernel efficiency change the opportunity for optimization. Compilation changes pruning and step-reduction savings, while pruning changes quantization benefits. VLA-Triage formalizes these findings into guidelines for selecting an execution mode, checking feasibility, and validating combinations under a deployment latency budget. The resulting guidance identifies when standalone measurements remain informative and when the combined execution must be measured.

The released DDIM sampler constructs its step schedule on the CPU during each step, preventing this loop from being recorded as a CUDA graph. Our replacement precomputes the same schedule. Across five seeds, the maximum absolute difference between its actions and those of the released loop is 1.2 × 10 − 6 1.2\times 10^{-6} in fp32 on CPU, using identical weights, noise and conditioning inputs.

We check that the expected input sequence for each model: 291 tokens for OpenVLA, 605 for OpenVLA-OFT (including 56 action slots), 276 for CogACT (including the cognition token), and 633 for LLaVA-VLA. We also check LLaVA-VLA’s token IDs against its released server using the same instruction.

We simulate LeRobot’s asynchronous action queue, which the robot drains at the control rate while the policy refills it with each inference, to compute how often a given inference time leaves the robot with no action to execute.

passages.location: Appendix B Runtimes, Software and Measurement Checks
passages.text: Timing begins with preprocessed camera frames and ends with actions, excluding CPU image preprocessing. CUDA events placed between modules divide inference into stages: host-to-device copy, vision encoder, projector, token selection where pruning is enabled, language-model prefill, then decoding for OpenVLA and LLaVA-VLA, the action head for OpenVLA-OFT and CogACT, or the denoising loop for the flow models, and postprocessing. Each stage time is the elapsed time between its two events on the GPU stream. Compilation uses torch.compile Ansel et al. () , and quantisation uses torchao torchao maintainers and contributors (2024) . Only the language-model linear layers of the Llama-based models are quantised. For each quantisation scheme and platform, we time the available library implementations and select the fastest one whose output error is within 1.25 times the smallest error measured for that quantisation scheme (Table 9 ).

passages.text: On x86 platforms, the Llama-based models and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} generally use PyTorch 2.7.1. The exceptions are quantised runs and compilation variants of the Llama-based models on the H100 and A10G, which use PyTorch 2.10 with torchao 0.13. The Thor uses this stack throughout. GR00T and SmolVLA use PyTorch 2.11 on x86 platforms and 2.10 on the Thor (Table 7 ). We do not report quantisation schemes on the RTX 4090.

When processing one request at a time, latency can depend on which CPU core launches GPU work. The protocol therefore pins the issuing thread to one core (Section 3 ). With pinning, OpenVLA’s eager rounds agree within 2.1%. Across identical configurations measured in separate jobs days apart, the median relative latency difference is 0.2% under CUDA graphs and 1.4% in eager execution. The 5.3% reporting cutoff is the largest eager baseline change observed when remeasuring the RTX 4090 at the end of its campaign. CUDA-graph latencies measured under the two software stacks in Table 7 agree within 4 ms. Recalculating each interaction example in Section 5 using every pairing of recorded baseline and optimized round medians preserves the reported direction. OpenVLA-OFT’s increase in pruning saving under CUDA graphs on the Thor remains positive in every pairing.

We compare kernel busy time from our CUPTI profiler with Nsight Systems, expressing differences relative to the CUPTI value. The differences are at most 0.12% on A10G and 2.1% under compilation and CUDA graphs on H100. For eager H100 runs, Nsight reports 4.7–12.2% more busy time and longer durations for short kernels. On Thor, the differences range from 0.8% to 2.1%, and both profilers give the same ordering for all 12 checked configurations.

passages.section: Appendix H Preference Order and Screening Consistency
passages.location: Appendix H Preference Order and Screening Consistency
passages.text: Table 17 lists the recorded settings that meet the inference-time budget for each over-budget model–platform case, using a fixed preference order. For pruning, select the lowest percentage of tokens removed that meets the budget. For quantization, consider groups in this order: int8 weights, int4 weights, 8-bit compute (int8, dynamic FP8 or static FP8), then NVFP4. Select the fastest scheme in the first group containing a budget-meeting option. Consider pairs only when neither method meets the budget alone, ordered by pruning level, then quantization group, then latency. This order is fixed solely to make the comparison on the recorded grid reproducible. It does not rank task accuracy or prescribe a quantization order for deployment. Each case uses one execution mode and only the settings recorded in it. Pruning uses random token selection; recorded levels vary by platform, with 6.25% increments on RTX 4090. H100 and A10G cases use the PyTorch 2.10 and torchao 0.13 campaign, while LLaVA-VLA compilation and the other platforms retain earlier records.

On the three cases whose selected mode is CUDA graphs, it excludes pruning alone in two, and neither has a pruning level meeting the budget. Because the compiled cases lack this measurement, Table 16 instead removes each affected stage entirely, counting prefill plus decode for autoregressive pruning. This weaker form excludes nothing on the grid. The weight-read screen excludes candidates in four cases, and each excluded candidate’s own measured latency, after its pruning or quantization, is at least 2.67 ​ B 2.67B (median 6.67 ​ B 6.67B ). This audit does not test how well the screens distinguish candidates close to the budget. The weight-read bound assumes unchanged layer counts, at least 4-bit weights, and mandatory weight streaming from DRAM on each pass without inter-pass cache reuse. These assumptions must be checked before using the bound to exclude a deployment candidate. Table 16 gives the counts for each search strategy.
